title: Try a new case
subtitle: An optional written transfer check after the ten chapters
intro: Try this fictional case without your notes. Allow twenty to thirty minutes. Write somewhere private; this page does not collect or grade your answers. Compare with the suggested reasoning after your attempt.
paragraphs: A museum offers a family workshop. A toddler watches an unexpected toy event for longer. A guide calls this proof of advanced intelligence and labels a nearby child insecure because the child stays close to a caregiver.

A child sorts objects with a prompt but struggles with a new unprompted example. A bilingual visitor says little in English. An adolescent volunteer checks carefully in rehearsal and rushes during a public demonstration.

An older volunteer knows the exhibits but struggles with a small-print digital menu. A coordinator compares current teenagers with current older adults and calls the difference a pure age effect. A parent returns to study and is described as behind schedule.
The museum wants inclusive support and evidence that learning lasts. It has not measured prior experience, task access or later independent performance.

tasks.title: Age and historical context
tasks.prompt: Explain two limits of the age comparison and the claim about being behind schedule.
tasks.answer: Age groups differ in prior experience and historical opportunities. Cross-sectional differences do not isolate within-person change. A cultural timetable is not a universal developmental requirement.

tasks.title: Early development and relationships
tasks.prompt: Separate the toddler’s observation from the intelligence inference and assess the attachment label. Explain why early risks do not determine a future.
tasks.answer: Longer looking is an indirect attention measure with alternative explanations. One visit cannot classify attachment. Early exposures and relationships can alter probabilities without fixing individual outcomes; timing, dose and context matter.

tasks.title: Learning and participation
tasks.prompt: What would distinguish supported from independent learning? How should the language observation be interpreted?
tasks.answer: Fade the prompt and use a new suitable example. Assess later independent use. One English conversation misses language knowledge across contexts; examine instructions, relationships and linguistic access before judging ability.

tasks.title: Adolescence and ageing
tasks.prompt: Recommend two task-specific supports without diagnosing or excluding anyone by age.
tasks.answer: Rehearse the public task with clear safety boundaries and appropriate supervision. Improve display access and provide an accurate sequence. Context and experience matter; persistent concerning daily-life changes warrant qualified assessment.

tasks.title: Evaluate the workshop
tasks.prompt: Design a proportionate test and state an ethical limit.
tasks.answer: Specify a learning outcome, compare comparable supports, account for experience and access, then check delayed unfamiliar performance. Obtain appropriate consent and protect privacy; do not conduct informal diagnostic tests or experiments on children.

rubric.title: Accurate distinctions
rubric.strong: Explains the relevant concepts and separates observations from interpretations.
rubric.developing: Adds labels without explaining how the evidence supports them.

rubric.title: Evidence and alternatives
rubric.strong: Considers competing explanations and a comparison that could distinguish them.
rubric.developing: Treats a plausible account, score or correlation as a settled cause.

rubric.title: Proportionate application
rubric.strong: States limitations, respects the people involved and explains what would change the recommendation.
rubric.developing: Overgeneralizes to individuals or makes a recommendation beyond the evidence.

followup: Return tomorrow or in a week with an unfamiliar example. Compare the quality of your explanation, not just your confidence. This self-check does not certify professional competence or establish general mastery.
